around.headline: Cyberfraud gang busted with 507 mule bank accounts
around.summary: Police arrested three men found with 507 mule bank accounts on their phones, used to shuttle money stolen in cyber scams, per The Times of India. Never let anyone else use your bank account or UPI ID to move money for a fee — you can be held liable as the account holder even if you didn't run the scam.

around.headline: Spurious-drug crackdown widens: 16 pharmacy licences cancelled, Rs 5 crore fake stock seized
around.summary: Karnataka's FDA cancelled 16 retailer and wholesaler licences and the health minister ordered action against 24 more pharma traders, days after a Rs 5 crore counterfeit-medicine haul was seized at a Bidadi farmhouse, per The Hindu, Deccan Chronicle and The Times of India. Buy medicines only from licensed pharmacies and check for a clear batch number and QR code on the strip.
around.source: The Hindu, The Times of India

around.headline: Record 10.99 lakh wrong-parking cases booked, but menace continues
around.summary: Bengaluru traffic police have booked a record 10.99 lakh wrong-parking cases this year, yet illegal parking keeps choking roads, per The Hindu. Expect stepped-up camera enforcement — double-check before leaving your vehicle on a no-parking stretch.

around.headline: BMTC's Rs 40 crore digital ETA boards at bus stops go dark
around.summary: The New Indian Express reports that Rs 40 crore worth of digital bus-arrival display boards across the city have stopped working, leaving commuters without real-time ETAs. Until they're fixed, use the Namma BMTC 2.0 app (now also on iPhone) for live bus timings instead of the boards.
around.source: The New Indian Express, The Hindu

around.headline: New 'software charge' on property tax draws backlash from owners
around.summary: The Greater Bengaluru Authority has added a fresh 'software charge' on top of property tax bills, prompting anger from property owners, per Deccan Herald, The Hindu and Bangalore Mirror. Check your latest property tax notice carefully for this new line item before paying.

around.headline: Landslide and flash floods kill 6 in Kerala amid heavy rain alert
around.summary: A landslide and flash floods killed six people in Kerala as authorities issued a heavy rain warning, per The Times of India. With Bengaluru itself at a 93% rain chance today, avoid low-lying underpasses and hillside routes during any heavy downpour.

street_smart.title: A neighbour's cousin, whom you've met a couple of times at local gatherings, asks if he can deposit ₹40,000 cash into your bank account for a day and transfer it out tomorrow, offering you ₹1,000 for the favour — like the mule-account network police busted in Bengaluru today, where 507 such accounts were used to move cyberfraud money. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: The Times of India, Sept 21 — a Bengaluru cyberfraud gang was busted with 507 mule bank accounts found across the phones of 3 accused, used to shuttle scammed money through unsuspecting or willing account holders. This bank-account-mule-recruitment mechanism hasn't been used as a street-smart scenario in the last three weeks.
street_smart.situation: He says it's just to help settle a shop payment quickly since his own account is 'under some bank issue', and he's a familiar, friendly face in the neighbourhood — not a stranger.

choices.text: Refuse and explain that you can't let anyone else's money move through your account, however small the ask or the fee offered.
choices.feedback: Correct. As the account holder, you're legally responsible for every transaction in your name — if that cash is later traced to a scam, your account gets frozen and you become a suspect, regardless of how well you know the person asking.

choices.text: Agree, since it's a small, one-day favour for someone you know and ₹1,000 is easy money.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. This is exactly the pitch behind mule-account recruitment — a familiar face, a small fee, a 'just for a day' promise. Once the money moves, you have no control over where it came from, and banks freeze the account first and ask questions later.

choices.text: Agree, but only after asking him to show you proof of where the cash came from.
choices.feedback: Risky. A verbal or even documented explanation from him proves nothing to your bank or the police — once funds routed through fraud land in your account, you're liable for it regardless of what he told you beforehand.

choices.text: Decline for yourself, but suggest he ask another relative's account instead since you don't want to get involved.
choices.feedback: Risky. Staying quiet doesn't stop the crime — it just moves the same risk onto someone else. If you suspect the request is a mule-account pitch, report it rather than just passing it along.

takeaways: Never let anyone else — friend, relative or stranger — use your bank account, UPI ID or ATM card to move money for a fee; you're liable as the account holder if it's later traced to fraud, even years afterward.
If someone pitches you cash-for-account-use, report it to the National Cyber Crime helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in — don't just decline quietly.
Banks can freeze an account under police investigation for months even when the holder is eventually cleared, since the account itself becomes evidence, not just the money in it.

quiz.question: Police in Bengaluru today busted a cyberfraud gang whose phones held how many mule bank accounts used to move scam money?
quiz.why: Mule accounts let fraud rings scatter stolen money across many names fast, making it harder for banks and police to trace and freeze before it's withdrawn.

quiz.question: Bengaluru's BMTC digital bus-arrival display boards, now reported non-functional across the city, cost roughly how much to install?
quiz.why: Until the boards are fixed, commuters are relying on the Namma BMTC 2.0 app, now also available on iPhone, for live arrival times.

quiz.question: A landslide and flash floods reported today killed how many people in Kerala amid a heavy rain alert?
quiz.why: Kerala's hilly, high-rainfall terrain makes it especially prone to landslides during intense monsoon spells, unlike Bengaluru's flatter plateau geography.

quiz.question: Heavy, rain-bearing overcast skies like Bengaluru's forecast today are most associated with which cloud type?
quiz.why: Nimbostratus clouds are thick, grey and cover the whole sky, producing the steady, prolonged rain typical of an overcast day — unlike the short, intense bursts from cumulonimbus storm clouds.

quiz.question: Bengaluru's municipal drinking water supply is drawn primarily from which river, pumped in from over 100 km away?
quiz.why: Cauvery water is lifted roughly 300 metres in elevation to reach the city, making Bengaluru's water supply one of the most energy-intensive in India.
